text: Whether matrimony between apostates from the faith and those previously rightly baptized, entered upon after the apostasy, publicly according to the custom of pagans or Mohammedans, is truly matrimony and a sacrament.
Reply: If any agreement of dissolubility be at hand, there is no matrimony and no sacrament, but if none is at hand, there is matrimony and a sacrament

topic: Haec Sancta: the authority of the council
source: [Translated for this site from the Latin text of the decree. A shorter form had been read at the fourth session; this is the form adopted at the fifth. Compare a critical edition before citing.]
text: This holy synod of Constance, forming a general council for the ending of the present schism and for the union and reform of the Church of God in head and members, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit to the praise of almighty God, in order that the union and reform of the Church of God may be obtained more easily, more securely, more fully and more freely, ordains, defines, enacts, decrees and declares as follows.

First, that this synod, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit, forming a general council and representing the Catholic Church militant, has its power immediately from Christ; and that everyone, of whatever state or dignity, even if it be papal, is bound to obey it in what pertains to the faith, to the ending of the said schism, and to the general reform of the said Church of God in head and members.

Next, it declares that anyone, of whatever condition, state or dignity, even if it be papal, who contumaciously refuses to obey the mandates, statutes, ordinances or precepts of this holy synod, or of any other general council lawfully assembled, on the matters named above or on what pertains to them, whether already made or to be made, shall, unless he repents, be subjected to fitting penance and duly punished, recourse being had, if necessary, to other aids of the law.

source: [Summary written for this site; the texts are not reproduced.]
text: Session 12 (29 May 1415) deposed John XXIII, the Pisan claimant, and decreed that none of the three claimants could be elected pope again.

Session 14 (4 July 1415): Gregory XII, the Roman claimant, through his representative first convoked the assembly as a general council and then resigned. The council accepted the resignation and kept his cardinals and officials in their dignities.
Session 37 (26 July 1417) deposed Peter de Luna, called Benedict XIII, the Avignon claimant, who refused to resign.
Session 41 (8 November 1417) opened the conclave, and Martin V was elected on 11 November 1417, ending the schism.

topic: Against leaving, disturbing or violating the council before the election
source: [Decree of session 14. Hardt, Magnum Oecumenicum Constantiense Concilium III (1698), p. 378. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Likewise, the most holy general synod of Constance, etc. In order that, before the election of the future Roman supreme Pontiff and the other business to be conducted in the same Council, the sacred Council itself may not be dissolved or disturbed, nor anything plotted against its welfare or prosperity, nor its holy statutes and ordinances in any way molested, violated or transgressed, it statutes, ordains and defines the following.

Whoever, of whatever status, dignity, rank, order or preeminence, shall henceforth depart from this holy Council without the license of the Council itself, or of those deputed for this purpose, and whatever member of the Council or any other person shall in any way disturb the Council itself, or plot anything against its welfare or prosperity, or rashly violate, break or transgress the statutes and ordinances of this sacred Council, especially those made in the present session, shall be considered one who disturbs the union, sows schism, and is suspect of heresy and of the crime of offense against majesty.

Such a person shall be perpetually infamous and deprived by the law itself of every dignity, honor, status, office and benefice, ecclesiastical and secular, whether Imperial, Royal, Cardinalatial or Pontifical, with all hope of promotion entirely removed. Nor shall the door to any dignity or honor, ecclesiastical or worldly, be opened to him.

source: [Summary of the decree's provisions written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: Frequent general councils are the chief means of tending the Lord's field: they root out heresy, error and schism, correct excesses and reform what is deformed. Neglecting them lets these evils grow.
The next council is to meet five years after the end of this one, the following one seven years after that, and from then on one every ten years, for ever.

The pope, with the consent and approval of the council, is to name the place of the next council a month before each council ends; if he fails to, the council itself names it. So there is always either a council in session or one due at a fixed term.

The pope may shorten an interval for an urgent reason, with the advice of his cardinals, but may never lengthen it. The place may not be changed except for clear necessity such as siege, war or plague, and then only to a suitable place nearby, with the consent of two thirds of the cardinals, announced a year ahead.

topic: Future schisms and the pope's profession of faith
source: [Summary written for this site; the texts are not reproduced.]
text: Against future schisms: if a schism arises, the next council is to meet within a year without further summons; from its opening every claimant is suspended from administration, and a papal election made under fear or force is void.

The profession of the pope: a newly elected pope is to profess, before his election is published, that he holds the Catholic faith as handed down by the apostles and the general councils (naming the eight ecumenical councils and those of Lateran, Lyons and Vienne), and that he will keep it to the end.
Further decrees forbade translating prelates against their will and limited the papal claim to the spoils of deceased clergy and to procurations.

topic: Electing the pope and the reform programme
source: [Summary written for this site; the texts are not reproduced.]
text: For this election only, the cardinals were joined by six deputies from each of the council's five nations, and the one elected needed two thirds of the cardinals and two thirds of each nation's deputies.

The new pope was bound, with the council, to reform the Church in head and in the Roman curia on eighteen listed points before the council was dissolved, among them the number of cardinals, reservations, annates, appeals to the curia, simony, dispensations, and the grounds on which a pope may be corrected or deposed.

topic: Martin V releases Baldassare Cossa, formerly John XXIII
source: [Bull of Martin V, read in session 42. Latin in Mansi 27, col. 1172; Hardt, Magnum Oecumenicum Constantiense Concilium IV (1699), col. 1500; Monumenta Conciliorum Generalium III/1, 1185. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Latin opening: "Dudum præsens sacrum generale Concilium Constantiense personam Baltassaris Cossa, olim Joannis Papæ vigesimitertii in sua obedientia nuncupati, post illius a papatu per definitivam sententiam ejusdem Concilii canonicam depositionem per eamdem sententiam…"

Formerly the present holy general Council of Constance condemned the person of Balthasar Cossa, formerly called Pope John XXIII in his obedience, after his canonical deposition from the papacy by the definitive sentence of the same Council, by that same sentence, to stand and to remain in some good and honest place, under custody and safekeeping in the name of the said holy Council, for as long as it should seem good to the same holy Council for the good of the union of the Church of God: whom hitherto you have faithfully and diligently preserved, both through you and through our beloved son, the noble man Louis, Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine, in your name, under trust and safe custody, honorably and duly, as a zealot and devoted servant of union and peace…
The bull provides for his release from that custody. Cossa was freed in 1419, submitted to Martin V at Florence, was made cardinal bishop of Tusculum, and died that December.

source: [Summary written for this site; the texts are not reproduced.]
text: Martin V and the council revoked exemptions granted since the schism, and unions and incorporations of benefices made without cause.

They reserved the income of vacant benefices to their proper uses, renewed the penalties against simony, limited dispensations, restricted papal taxes on the clergy, and set rules for the life, dress and conduct of clerics. Other reforms were left to concordats with the nations.

topic: Martin V: what the council did "conciliariter" in matters of faith
source: [Martin V's reply to the Polish envoys Gaspar of Perugia and Paweł Włodkowic, who pressed for a conciliar condemnation of John Falkenberg's writings. Hardt IV (1699), col. 1557. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Latin: "…imposito omnibus silentio, dixit, respondendo ad praedicta, quod omnia et singula determinata et conclusa et decreta in materiis fidei per praesens concilium conciliariter tenere et inviolabiliter observare volebat et nunquam contravenire quoquo modo. Ipsaque sic conciliariter facta approbat omnia gesta in concilio conciliariter circa materiam fidei et ratificat et non aliter nec alio modo."

…silence having been imposed on all, he said, responding to the aforesaid things, that he wished to hold, and inviolably to observe, all and each of the things determined, concluded and decreed in matters of faith by the present council, conciliarly, and never to contravene them in any way. And he approves all things thus done conciliarly, all things enacted in the council conciliarly concerning the matter of faith, and ratifies them, and not otherwise nor in another manner.

source: [Summary written for this site.]
text: Martin V confirmed the condemnations of Wycliffe and Hus in the bull Inter Cunctas (see n. 657 ff.).
In a consistory of 10 March 1418 he rejected any appeal from the Apostolic See to a future council.

At the last session (22 April 1418) he declared that he approved and ratified what the council had decided conciliariter, as a council, in matters of faith (C9). Whether this covered Haec Sancta is disputed; the usual Catholic reading is that it did not.

He treated the council's acts on the schism as settled: Cossa's deposition was "canonical" (C8), the Pisan pope Alexander V is "our predecessor" in his register (C10), and the next council was forbidden to reopen the depositions or his election (C11). He praised the king of Poland for holding that there is no appeal from the Roman Bishop (C12).

In 1446–1447, in negotiations with the German princes, Eugene IV received Constance and Frequens, and Basel up to its transfer, without prejudice to the rights of the Apostolic See (B13–B15), and Nicholas V confirmed the concessions (B16). Pius II forbade appeals from the pope to a future council (n. 717), and Lateran V and Vatican I taught the pope's authority over councils (n. 740, 1830–1831).

topic: Martin V names Alexander V "our predecessor"
source: [Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Reg. Lat. 187, fol. 1, 1v, a confirmation at the opening of Martin V's register. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Latin: "Alexander papa V predecessor noster … et deinde Baldassar tunc Johannes papa XXIII, qui dicto predecessore ab hac luce sublato in papatu immediate successit … nobis, qui post depositionem dicti Baldassaris a papatu fuimus divina favente clementia ad apicem summi apostolatus assumpti."

Pope Alexander V, our predecessor … and then Baldassarre, at that time Pope John XXIII, who, when the said predecessor was taken from this life, immediately succeeded him in the papacy … we, who after the deposition of the said Baldassarre from the papacy were, by the favor of divine mercy, raised to the summit of the supreme apostolate.

topic: Martin V to the Council of Pavia–Siena: Constance's acts on the schism are not to be questioned
source: [Martin V's instructions for the council called under Frequens. Mansi 28, col. 1080. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: In such a manner, however, that it shall not hereby be understood that permission has been granted to call into question what was wholesomely defined by the sacred Council of Constance regarding the sedition of the past schism, the deposition of those who were then contending for the papacy, and the inspired elevation of this same Lord our Pope to the apostolate, or to propose or attempt anything in any way contrary to these decisions or any part of them.

topic: Martin V to Władysław II of Poland: no appeal from the Roman Bishop
source: [Archiv für österreichische Geschichte 45 (1871), 480. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: It has also found our pleasure, and brings it to expression, that the appeal to the next council lodged by your spokesmen at the Council of Constance has been withdrawn and rejected by your Highness after sound and mature deliberation, whereby you have shown your reverence towards us and your royal wisdom. For since satisfaction was sufficiently done to your honour by us, you have desisted from the unseemly appeal and have pronounced most rightly that there is no authority on earth whatsoever to which one might appeal from the Roman Bishop.

topic: Martin V to Alfonso V of Aragon: Constance represented the universal Church
source: [Raynald, Annales ecclesiastici IX (Lucca, 1752), ad annum 1426, n. 1. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Truly, whereas long ago through the inveterate and horrendous schism the holy Roman and universal Church, and the one body of those believing in Christ, monstrously divided under a triple head, was divided, and so great was the difficulty of union that for thirty-six years and more no human ingenuity could find it, although it was sought by the labors of many princes and prelates; at length the Lord, the single spouse of his holy Church, showing mercy and working by his Spirit to remove so detestable a monster from the Church of God, the general Council of Constance was gathered from every kingdom, nation and state of those believing in Christ, which represented the universal Church of God, at length united in itself, in which, first under two heads, since the whole weight of the schism rested on Pedro de Luna of damned memory, called Benedict XIII in his obedience, the aforesaid general council, proceeding duly against the same Peter, obstinate and pertinacious in the schism, declaratively sentenced him a notorious schismatic and heretic […]

topic: Synod of Tortosa under Martin V's legate: the schism and Constance recalled
source: [Synod of Tortosa (1429), presided over by Pierre de Foix, cardinal and legate of Martin V. Mansi 28, col. 1122. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, Amen. Let all present and future know that, whereas nearly fifty years have now passed since a grave schismatic division invaded the Roman Church and, alas, afflicted it as well as other churches throughout the world, recently twelve years or thereabouts have passed since, in the General Council of Constance gathered in the Holy Spirit, among other things Baldassarre Cossa, called John XXIII, and Pedro de Luna, called Benedict XIII, were deposed from all right that they claimed to have in the Papacy; and Angelo Correr, called Gregory XII in his obediences, yielded and renounced whatever right belonged to him in the Papacy itself; and our most holy father and lord in Christ, the lord Martin V, by divine providence Pope, was elevated to the height of the supreme Apostolate.

topic: Martin V to John II of Castile: Constance's reform chapters unchanged
source: [K. A. Fink, Die politische Korrespondenz Martins V. nach den Brevenregistern (Quellen und Forschungen aus italienischen Archiven und Bibliotheken), p. 222, n. 365. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Because indeed the aforesaid bishop made mention to us concerning a certain reformation of some chapters published in the sacred Council of Constance, as we told him, nothing has ever been altered by us.

topic: Basel renews the decrees of Constance
source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: After Eugene IV ordered the council dissolved, the assembly renewed the Constance decrees on the authority of general councils, declaring that a general council has its power immediately from Christ and that anyone, even the pope, must obey it in matters of faith, the ending of schism and reform.
It added that this council could not be dissolved, transferred or postponed by anyone, the pope included, without its own consent.

topic: Eugene IV, Dudum sacrum: the council recognized
source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: Under pressure from the council and the princes, Eugene IV withdrew his dissolution and declared that the council had been lawfully continued from its beginning and should proceed with its purposes: the uprooting of heresy, peace among Christians, and reform.

topic: Eugene IV to the council: "we yielded to you and assented to your decree"
source: [Letter of Eugene IV to the Council of Basel, after Dudum sacrum. Mansi 29, col. 579. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: Perhaps someone might think, from those things which preceded in earlier times, that our minds are not entirely without a cloud; but if anyone wishes to look rightly at whatever we commanded to be offered to you through our ambassadors, especially on this last occasion, he will sufficiently understand the serenity of our heart (if we may speak of ourselves).

Nor was it difficult for us to accomplish this, we who have always proceeded with you toward the same end, having dissented only on the place of holding the council, always saving piety… We desired peace, we desired the reformation of the Church: on account of this matter, not only did we yield to you, but we also assented through our letters to your decree, just as you dictated. After these things, to a greater degree (as we have said before), we opened our heart…

source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: The council renewed the Constance decree on the authority and power of general councils and ordered it published widely, so that no one could plead ignorance of it.

topic: The Compacts with the Hussites: the chalice for Bohemia
source: [Summary written for this site.]
text: In agreements made at Prague (1433) and solemnly promulgated at Iglau (5 July 1436), the council allowed the Utraquists of Bohemia and Moravia to receive Communion under both kinds, on condition that they also taught that Christ is received whole and entire under each kind, and settled their other demands on preaching, clerical property and the punishment of public sins.
Pius II declared the Compacts void in 1462.

topic: Union with the Greeks; Jews and converts
source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: The council approved plans for a council of union with the Greeks.

Its decree on Jews and neophytes ordered bishops to have Jews and others instructed by preaching, renewed earlier canonical restrictions on dealings between Jews and Christians, and required that converts be welcomed, instructed and protected in their property.

source: [Summary written for this site; the texts are not reproduced.]
text: Session 20 (22 January 1435): penalties against clerics living in concubinage; the faithful need not shun excommunicated persons unless they are named or notorious; interdicts are not to be imposed lightly.
Session 21 (9 June 1435): annates and similar payments to the curia abolished; rules for the reverent celebration of the divine office.

Session 23 (March 1436): rules for papal elections and an oath and profession to be made by the pope; the number of cardinals limited to twenty-four, with requirements of age and learning; papal reservations of benefices restricted.

topic: Eugene IV transfers the council to Ferrara
source: [Summary written for this site.]
text: By the bull Doctoris gentium (18 September 1437) Eugene IV transferred the council to Ferrara, to meet the Greeks, and confirmed the transfer on 30 December 1437. The minority at Basel, with the papal legates, followed him; the majority stayed and continued to meet.

source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: The assembly at Basel declared three propositions to be truths of Catholic faith: that a general council has power over the pope and everyone else; that the pope cannot dissolve, transfer or postpone a lawfully assembled general council without its consent; and that whoever obstinately opposes these truths is a heretic.

topic: Eugene IV "deposed" and Felix V elected
source: [Summary written for this site.]
text: The assembly declared Eugene IV deposed as a heretic and schismatic (25 June 1439) and elected Amadeus VIII of Savoy as Felix V (5 November 1439).

topic: Basel's decree on the Immaculate Conception
source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: The assembly declared the doctrine that Mary was never actually subject to original sin to be pious and in harmony with the Church's worship, the Catholic faith, right reason and Scripture, to be approved, held and embraced by all Catholics; it forbade preaching or teaching the contrary, and fixed the feast for 8 December.

topic: Moyses vir Dei: Florence condemns Basel
source: [Summary written for this site; the text is not reproduced.]
text: The Council of Florence, with Eugene IV, condemned the three propositions of Basel's thirty-third session as contrary to Scripture and the Fathers, and the sentence against Eugene as void.

The decree gives three grounds. Basel read the propositions in a sense contrary to Scripture, the Fathers and Constance itself; the Constance decrees Basel relied on were issued by only one of the three obediences, while the schism lasted; and in Basel's sense they would contradict Scripture and the Fathers.

It did not reject Constance, but held that Basel had twisted its decrees into a sense contrary to their true meaning. It declared Basel's acts since the transfer null and its leaders schismatics and heretics, subject to the penalties of law.

topic: Eugene IV's instructions to his legates: Constance and Basel received, saving the Apostolic See
source: [Raynald, Annales ecclesiastici XXVIII (Bar-le-Duc, 1874), p. 461. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: We, inclined by the supplications of the king and the electors, in imitation of the holy Fathers our predecessors (by adhering to whose footsteps we do not doubt that we offer an acceptable service to the divine majesty), just as they were accustomed to receive, embrace and venerate the general councils of their times duly instituted and canonically celebrated, so do we receive, embrace and venerate with all reverence and devotion the general councils of Constance and of Basel, from its beginning up to the translation made by us, without prejudice, however, to the right, dignity and preeminence of the Holy Apostolic See, nor to the power granted by Christ in the person of Blessed Peter to it and to the one canonically seated upon it.

topic: Eugene IV, Ad ea ex debito: Constance and Frequens received
source: [Mercati, Raccolta di Concordati I (1919), p. 160 in the archive.org scan. The text answers the German demand of the Diet of Frankfurt (1446), proposed by Frederick III, printed in W. Rossmann, Betrachtungen über das Zeitalter der Reformation (Jena, 1858), p. 389. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the scan.]
text: The demand: "Likewise, since the apostolic orators in the assembly of the princes of this diet of Frankfurt have professed in the stead and name of our Lord himself the authority, honor, power and eminence of the sacred general councils, as contained in the decree Frequens and other decrees of the Council of Constance renewed at Basel at the time when it was reputed throughout the world as an unquestioned council, our Most Holy Lord through his opportune letters shall approve and ratify such profession."

The answer: Moreover, we receive, embrace and venerate the general Council of Constance, the decree Frequens and its other decrees, just as all other councils representing the Catholic Church militant, along with their power, authority, honor and eminence, even as our other predecessors, from whose footsteps we by no means intend to deviate, have done.

topic: Eugene IV's protest: no prejudice to the Apostolic See
source: [Mercati, Raccolta di Concordati I (1919), p. 176 ("Protesta di Eugenio IV"); often called the Salvatoria. Summary written for this site; the text has not been checked.]
text: On the same day as the concessions, the dying pope declared that, unable to weigh everything in his illness and acting for the peace of the German Church, he did not intend by them to depart from the teaching of the Fathers or to prejudice the rights and authority of the Apostolic See, and that anything in them to that effect was to be held as not granted.

topic: Nicholas V confirms Eugene IV's concessions to the German nation
source: [Mercati, Raccolta di Concordati I (1919), pp. 176–177 ("Niccolò V approva e conferma le concessioni fatte da Eugenio IV alla Nazione Germanica"). Located from the volume's table of contents; the text has not been checked for this site.]
text: Three weeks after his election, Nicholas V approved and confirmed the concessions Eugene IV had made to the German nation in February 1447 (B14).

source: [Summary written for this site.]
text: Concordats with the German princes (1447–1448) settled the German Church's relation to Rome. The assembly moved to Lausanne in 1448. Felix V abdicated, and on 25 April 1449 the assembly recognized Nicholas V and declared itself dissolved.
In 1460 Pius II forbade appeals from the pope to a future council (n. 717), and Lateran V (1516) taught that the pope alone has authority to convoke, transfer and dissolve councils (n. 740).

topic: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, legate of Nicholas V, on Constance and papal deposition
source: [Oration "Sentio," delivered at Vienna as papal legate, against an appeal from the pope to a future council. Edited and translated by Michael von Cotta-Schønberg, Orations of Pope Pius II, 20 (2019; final version 2025), p. 178; Latin in L. A. Muratori, Anecdota II, p. 121, quoted by Mansi in Natalis Alexander, Historia ecclesiastica, ed. Roncaglia and Mansi, vol. 9 (Venice, 1776), p. 364. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the edition.]
text: But however it may be, it is clear that only in this one case is a certain and undoubted pope subject to a council: if somebody occupying the papacy falls into heresy, he immediately ceases to be pope and becomes less than any Christian. And if he is a schismatic, he cannot be called a pope, for either he suffers the same affliction or his right to the papacy is in doubt. As implied in the decree of Konstanz [Haec Sancta Synodus], a certain and undoubted pope may never be deposed by a council unless he has scandalised the universal Church, something that would be seen when many complained about him from various parts of the world. This could happen if the pope gave wives back to the priests, committed a blood crime, or introduced a new rite that displeased the community of the faithful. But nothing of this sort is happening now. So, in the present case, a council is not above the pope, and there is no [legitimate] cause for an appeal to it.

topic: Pius II, In minoribus agentes: "Reject Aeneas, accept Pius"
source: [Bull of retraction addressed to the University of Cologne. English from Reject Aeneas, Accept Pius: Selected Letters of Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini (Pope Pius II), introduced and translated by Thomas M. Izbicki, Gerald Christianson and Philip Krey (Washington, 2006), p. 406. Translation and citation contributed to this site; not yet checked against the book.]
text: With these authorities, we recognize the power and authority of a general council as it was declared and defined in our age at Constance when the ecumenical council was assembled there. For we revere the Council of Constance and all councils that were approved by our predecessors. We never have heard of an approved council that assembled without papal authority when there was an unquestioned Roman pontiff. The body of Christ is not without a head, and all power flows from the head into the members. This is our position, our sons. This we believe, and this we acknowledge. This we assert, already aged and established at the summit of the apostolate to defend the truth.
